2000.title: A half-point increase takes the US rate to 6.5%
2000.analysis: The FOMC lifted its target by half a percentage point to 6.5%. It judged that even faster productivity growth had yet to bring supply into line with spending. All three institutions raised rates that year, with the euro-area deposit rate recording the largest cumulative increase.

2001.title: A rate cut as US financial markets reopen
2001.analysis: On the day US stock markets reopened after the September attacks, the Fed cut its target to 3% and pledged to keep supplying extraordinary liquidity to financial markets. Restoring payments and supporting demand called for different operations. The dated moves show that US easing was already well under way before September.

2002.title: Uncertainty about demand brings another US cut
2002.analysis: The Fed lowered its target by 50 basis points to 1.25%. It saw unusually high uncertainty restraining investment, production and hiring, even though productivity was rising. The ECB’s deposit rate also fell 50 basis points over the year. The UK repo rate remained at 4%.

2003.title: A UK hike disappears in the annual net change
2003.analysis: The MPC raised the repo rate to 3.75%, pointing to strong credit growth and a smaller slowdown in housing and consumer spending than it had expected. Two earlier cuts outweighed November’s increase. The UK’s lower closing rate therefore conceals a change in policy direction that is visible in the dated moves.

2004.title: The first move away from a 1% US target
2004.analysis: The FOMC raised its target to 1.25% and linked the expected pace of further increases to its inflation outlook. By year-end the target had reached 2.25%. The UK also raised rates over the year, while the ECB’s overnight deposit rate held at 1%.

2005.title: The UK cuts while the US keeps raising rates
2005.analysis: The MPC reduced its repo rate to 4.5%. Spending by households and growth in business investment had slowed. Although higher oil prices threatened near-term inflation, weaker domestic demand weighed on the medium-term forecast. The US target rose two full percentage points over the same calendar year.

2006.title: Three ECB rates rise together
2006.analysis: The ECB announced a quarter-point rise in all three policy rates. On 13 December the overnight deposit rate became 2.50%, the main refinancing minimum bid rate 3.50% and the marginal lending rate 4.50%. Their common direction masks their different functions. This series follows the price paid on overnight deposits throughout.

2007.title: Northern Rock receives institution-specific support
2007.analysis: The Chancellor authorised the Bank to lend to Northern Rock against collateral at a premium. The facility addressed the lender’s difficulty obtaining wholesale funding. Bank Rate still stood at 5.75% and its first cut came in December. A liquidity backstop could therefore operate while the general rate set for the economy stayed in place.

2008.title: The Fed replaces a point target with a range
2008.analysis: The FOMC moved from a 1% target to a 0–0.25% range and shifted attention to its balance sheet. Expressing the new band as a midpoint puts the December step at −87.5 basis points. The half basis point in the annual total follows from that measurement choice. The UK and euro-area instruments remain single rates.

2009.title: The UK adds asset purchases at 0.5%
2009.analysis: The MPC cut Bank Rate to 0.5% and voted to purchase £75 billion of assets using newly created central-bank reserves. The cut changed the overnight rate. Purchases added a channel through longer-term asset prices and financing conditions. The UK rate then stayed at 0.5% for the rest of the year.

2010.title: Three flat rate paths, a larger US purchase programme
2010.analysis: All three ledger rates finished where they started, without a single intervening change. The Fed nevertheless judged the recovery in employment and underlying inflation below its objectives. It announced plans to buy another $600 billion of longer-term Treasuries by mid-2011. A zero in the rate column leaves that commitment invisible.

2011.title: The ECB’s tightening and easing cancel out
2011.analysis: July’s decision put the deposit rate at 0.75% from 13 July, following an earlier spring rise. November and December cuts returned it to 0.25%. All three banks ended 2011 at their starting rates. Only the euro-area deposit series travelled 100 basis points between those endpoints.

2012.title: Lending determines access to cheaper bank funding
2012.analysis: The Bank and the Treasury announced a scheme that offered participating banks and building societies funding on terms linked to how much they lent to the UK real economy. The aim was to improve the transmission of monetary policy to borrowers. Bank Rate held at 0.5% throughout the year.

2013.title: UK guidance gives unemployment a policy role
2013.analysis: The MPC linked its earliest potential rate increase to unemployment falling to 7%, subject to safeguards for inflation and financial stability. Reaching the threshold would prompt reassessment. Guidance changed how households and markets could interpret labour data during a year with no rate changes in any of the three economies.

2014.title: The euro-area deposit facility crosses zero
2014.analysis: The ECB set the deposit facility rate at −0.10% with effect from 11 June. Banks using the facility would pay to leave funds overnight. September brought a second ten-basis-point cut. Both US and UK policy rates stayed above zero and unchanged throughout the year.

2015.title: Euro-area purchases expand to public-sector bonds
2015.analysis: The ECB announced that purchases would include euro-area public-sector bonds and that combined monthly purchases would reach €60 billion. The programme sought to ease borrowing conditions when the overnight deposit rate was already negative. The deposit rate fell further in December, the same month the US moved its target range up.

2016.title: UK easing combines three routes to borrowers
2016.instrument: Bank Rate, term funding and asset purchases
2016.analysis: Following the referendum on EU membership, the MPC cut Bank Rate to 0.25%, introduced funding for banks to help pass on the cut and expanded purchases to include corporate bonds. These decisions targeted overnight rates, banks’ funding costs and market borrowing costs. US rates moved in the opposite direction in December.

2017.title: US balance-sheet runoff gets a start date
2017.analysis: The FOMC held its target range at the September meeting and announced that the previously described balance-sheet normalisation programme would begin in October. Allowing some maturing assets to run off gradually reduced its holdings. Separately, three rate increases lifted the US midpoint by 75 basis points over the year.

2018.title: Ending net purchases leaves reinvestment in place
2018.analysis: The ECB confirmed that net purchases under its asset purchase programme would end in December. It intended to reinvest all principal payments from maturing securities well beyond the first rate increase. The purchase flow could slow to zero while the stock of securities continued to support financing conditions. The deposit rate stayed at −0.40%.

2019.title: Further euro-area easing changes reserve remuneration
2019.instrument: Deposit rate, reserve tiering and purchases
2019.analysis: The ECB cut the deposit rate to −0.50%, announced renewed net purchases of €20 billion a month from November and introduced a two-tier system for remunerating excess reserves. The exemption for part of banks’ holdings meant that the posted deposit rate alone could not describe what they paid across all their reserves.

2020.title: An emergency purchase envelope moves without a rate cut
2020.analysis: The ECB announced a €750 billion purchase envelope with flexibility across time, asset classes and jurisdictions. It sought to keep pandemic disruption from impairing the transmission of monetary policy across the currency union. The euro-area deposit rate stayed at −0.50% all year as the US and UK cut their rates sharply.

2021.title: The UK moves first among these three rate series
2021.analysis: The MPC raised Bank Rate from 0.10% to 0.25%. It weighed evidence of a tight labour market and more persistent cost pressures alongside uncertainty about Omicron. That 15-basis-point step was the only rate change across the three recorded instruments in 2021. The following year brought increases in all three.

2022.title: Gilt purchases during a tightening cycle
2022.analysis: The Bank announced time-limited purchases of long-dated UK government bonds to restore orderly trading amid severe market dysfunction. This intervention served a financial-stability purpose. Bank Rate rose by 325 basis points over the calendar year. Treating every asset purchase as evidence of a change in the MPC’s inflation stance would misread this episode.

2023.title: The ECB shifts attention to the duration of restraint
2023.analysis: The ECB announced a quarter-point increase in the deposit rate to 4.00% from 20 September. Its assessment placed weight on how long rates would stay at levels sufficient to bring inflation back to target. The euro-area rise over the year reached 200 basis points, compared with 175 in the UK and 100 in the US.

2024.title: A half-point US cut as employment risks gain weight
2024.analysis: The Fed lowered its target range to 4.75–5.00%. It judged that inflation had made progress and the risks to its employment and inflation goals were roughly balanced. The US and euro-area rates each ended a full percentage point below their starting values. Their cuts arrived at different times during the year.

2025.title: The ECB cuts as its inflation projections fall
2025.analysis: The ECB announced a reduction to 2.00% effective 11 June. It lowered its inflation projections for 2025 and 2026, citing weaker energy prices and a stronger euro. All three institutions lowered their rates during the year. The UK and euro-area series each fell 100 basis points, compared with 75 at the Fed.

2026.title: Rising energy costs return to the UK rate decision
2026.analysis: Eight MPC members voted to raise Bank Rate to 4%, and one favoured a larger increase. The committee judged that higher energy costs and stronger activity warranted tightening even with limited evidence so far of spillovers into wages and other prices. The three rate series had all risen by the November observation date.
